        <h1><i class="fas fa-search-plus"></i> ISO 27001:2022 Gap Analysis Guide</h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">Complete Assessment Framework for Compliance

        <h2 id="introduction">1. What is ISO 27001:2022 Gap Analysis?</h2>
        <p>
            An ISO 27001 gap analysis is a systematic comparison between your organization's current information
            security posture and the requirements of the ISO 27001:2022 standard. Think of it as a health check for
            your security program that reveals exactly where you stand and what needs improvement before pursuing
            certification.
        </p>
        <p>
            The gap analysis answers three critical questions:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Where are we now?</strong> Current state of security controls and processes</li>
            <li><strong>Where do we need to be?</strong> ISO 27001:2022 requirements and expectations</li>
            <li><strong>What's the gap?</strong> The delta between current state and compliance requirements</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Why Gap Analysis First?</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                Organizations that skip gap analysis spend an average of 40% more time on implementation. The gap
                analysis provides a roadmap that prevents wasted effort on controls you already have while
                highlighting critical blind spots.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h3>When to Conduct a Gap Analysis</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Scenario</th>
                    <th>Gap Analysis Purpose</th>
                    <th>Typical Duration</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>First-time certification</strong></td>
                    <td>Baseline assessment, implementation roadmap</td>
                    <td>2-4 weeks</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Transition from 2013 to 2022</strong></td>
                    <td>Identify new controls, mapping existing controls</td>
                    <td>1-2 weeks</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Post-acquisition/merger</strong></td>
                    <td>Assess inherited systems and processes</td>
                    <td>3-6 weeks</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Pre-audit health check</strong></td>
                    <td>Identify gaps before certification body arrives</td>
                    <td>1 week</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Annual review</strong></td>
                    <td>Continuous improvement, maintain compliance</td>
                    <td>3-5 days</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="changes-2022">2. Key Changes: ISO 27001:2013 vs 2022</h2>
        <p>
            The 2022 revision brought significant restructuring to Annex A. Understanding these changes is essential
            for anyone familiar with the previous version.
        </p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Aspect</th>
                    <th>ISO 27001:2013</th>
                    <th>ISO 27001:2022</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Total Controls</strong></td>
                    <td>114 controls</td>
                    <td>93 controls</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Control Domains</strong></td>
                    <td>14 domains (A.5 - A.18)</td>
                    <td>4 themes</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>New Controls</strong></td>
                    <td>-</td>
                    <td>11 new controls</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Merged Controls</strong></td>
                    <td>-</td>
                    <td>24 controls merged</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Control Attributes</strong></td>
                    <td>Not included</td>
                    <td>5 attribute types for each control</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Transition Deadline</strong></td>
                    <td>-</td>
                    <td>October 31, 2025</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>The 11 New Controls in ISO 27001:2022</h3>
        <p>
            These controls reflect modern security challenges that didn't exist or weren't prominent in 2013:
        </p>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Control ID</th>
                    <th>Control Name</th>
                    <th>Why It's New</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.5.7</td>
                    <td>Threat Intelligence</td>
                    <td>Proactive threat awareness</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.5.23</td>
                    <td>Information Security for Cloud Services</td>
                    <td>Cloud adoption explosion</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.5.30</td>
                    <td>ICT Readiness for Business Continuity</td>
                    <td>Technology resilience focus</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.7.4</td>
                    <td>Physical Security Monitoring</td>
                    <td>Surveillance and detection</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.9</td>
                    <td>Configuration Management</td>
                    <td>Baseline security settings</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.10</td>
                    <td>Information Deletion</td>
                    <td>Data lifecycle management</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.11</td>
                    <td>Data Masking</td>
                    <td>Privacy and data protection</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.12</td>
                    <td>Data Leakage Prevention</td>
                    <td>DLP requirements</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.16</td>
                    <td>Monitoring Activities</td>
                    <td>Detection and SIEM</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.23</td>
                    <td>Web Filtering</td>
                    <td>Content filtering controls</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>A.8.28</td>
                    <td>Secure Coding</td>
                    <td>Application security focus</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Transition Deadline</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                All certified organizations must transition to ISO 27001:2022 by <strong>October 31, 2025</strong>.
                Certifications under the 2013 version will not be valid after this date.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="methodology">3. Gap Analysis Methodology</h2>
        <p>
            A structured methodology ensures consistent, repeatable assessments. Here's a proven five-phase
            approach:
        </p>

        <h3>Phase 1: Scope Definition</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Define ISMS boundaries (business units, locations, systems)</li>
            <li>Identify key stakeholders and process owners</li>
            <li>Gather existing documentation (policies, procedures, risk assessments)</li>
            <li>Establish assessment timeline and resources</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Phase 2: Document Review</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Review existing ISMS documentation against ISO 27001 requirements</li>
            <li>Assess policy completeness and currency</li>
            <li>Evaluate procedure alignment with controls</li>
            <li>Check evidence of implementation and records</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Phase 3: Control Assessment</h3>
        <p>For each of the 93 Annex A controls, evaluate:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Implementation Status:</strong> Not implemented, Partially, Fully implemented</li>
            <li><strong>Evidence Quality:</strong> None, Informal, Documented, Proven effective</li>
            <li><strong>Gap Severity:</strong> Critical, High, Medium, Low</li>
            <li><strong>Remediation Effort:</strong> Quick win, Moderate, Significant project</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Phase 4: Stakeholder Interviews</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Interview process owners to validate document review findings</li>
            <li>Observe actual practices vs documented procedures</li>
            <li>Identify undocumented but effective controls</li>
            <li>Uncover cultural and awareness gaps</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Phase 5: Reporting and Roadmap</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Compile findings into gap analysis report</li>
            <li>Prioritize gaps by risk and remediation effort</li>
            <li>Create remediation timeline with milestones</li>
            <li>Estimate resource requirements and budget</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Best Practice: Evidence-Based Assessment</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                Never rely solely on interviews. For each control, request evidence: screenshots, logs, policy
                documents, training records. "We do that" isn't evidence; a signed procedure with audit trail is.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="annex-a-themes">4. The Four Annex A Themes (93 Controls)</h2>
        <p>
            ISO 27001:2022 restructured the 93 controls into four logical themes. Understanding this structure helps
            organize your assessment and responsibilities.
        </p>

        <div class="theme-grid">
            <div class="theme-card organizational">
                <h4 style="color: var(--accent-blue);"><i class="fas fa-building"></i> Organizational Controls</h4>
                <div class="count" style="color: var(--accent-blue);">37 <span>controls</span></div>
                <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary); font-size: 0.95rem;">
                    Policies, roles, responsibilities, asset management, access control, supplier relationships,
                    incident management, business continuity, compliance
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="theme-card people">
                <h4 style="color: var(--accent-green);"><i class="fas fa-users"></i> People Controls</h4>
                <div class="count" style="color: var(--accent-green);">8 <span>controls</span></div>
                <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary); font-size: 0.95rem;">
                    Screening, employment terms, awareness training, disciplinary process, termination, remote
                    working, event reporting
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="theme-card physical">
                <h4 style="color: var(--accent-orange);"><i class="fas fa-door-closed"></i> Physical Controls</h4>
                <div class="count" style="color: var(--accent-orange);">14 <span>controls</span></div>
                <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary); font-size: 0.95rem;">
                    Physical perimeters, entry controls, securing offices, monitoring, protecting against threats,
                    equipment security, secure disposal, clear desk
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="theme-card technological">
                <h4 style="color: var(--accent-blue);"><i class="fas fa-microchip"></i> Technological Controls
                </h4>
                <div class="count" style="color: var(--accent-blue);">34 <span>controls</span></div>
                <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary); font-size: 0.95rem;">
                    Endpoint devices, access rights, authentication, malware, backups, logging, monitoring,
                    network security, cryptography, secure development, testing
                </p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Organizational Controls (A.5) - Key Areas</h3>
        <p>These 37 controls form the foundation of your ISMS:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>A.5.1-A.5.6:</strong> Policies and roles - Governance structure</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.7:</strong> Threat intelligence - NEW in 2022</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.9-A.5.14:</strong> Asset management - Classification and handling</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.15-A.5.18:</strong> Access control - Identity and access management</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.19-A.5.22:</strong> Supplier relationships - Third-party risk</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.23-A.5.25:</strong> Cloud security - NEW emphasis in 2022</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.24-A.5.28:</strong> Incident management - Detection and response</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.29-A.5.30:</strong> Business continuity - Resilience</li>
            <li><strong>A.5.31-A.5.37:</strong> Compliance - Legal and contractual</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>People Controls (A.6) - Key Areas</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>A.6.1:</strong> Background screening before employment</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.2:</strong> Terms and conditions of employment</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.3:</strong> Information security awareness, education, and training</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.4:</strong> Disciplinary process for violations</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.5:</strong> Responsibilities after termination</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.6:</strong> Confidentiality agreements</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.7:</strong> Remote working security</li>
            <li><strong>A.6.8:</strong> Security event reporting</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Physical Controls (A.7) - Key Areas</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>A.7.1-A.7.3:</strong> Physical security perimeters and entry</li>
            <li><strong>A.7.4:</strong> Physical security monitoring - NEW in 2022</li>
            <li><strong>A.7.5-A.7.8:</strong> Protecting against environmental threats</li>
            <li><strong>A.7.9-A.7.13:</strong> Equipment security and maintenance</li>
            <li><strong>A.7.14:</strong> Secure disposal or reuse of equipment</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Technological Controls (A.8) - Key Areas</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>A.8.1-A.8.8:</strong> Endpoint and access management</li>
            <li><strong>A.8.9-A.8.12:</strong> Configuration, deletion, masking, DLP - NEW controls</li>
            <li><strong>A.8.13-A.8.17:</strong> Backup, redundancy, logging, monitoring</li>
            <li><strong>A.8.18-A.8.22:</strong> Network security and segregation</li>
            <li><strong>A.8.23-A.8.25:</strong> Web filtering, cryptography - NEW/enhanced</li>
            <li><strong>A.8.26-A.8.34:</strong> Application security, secure development, testing</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="commonly-failed">5. Most Commonly Failed Controls</h2>
        <p>
            Based on analysis of hundreds of certification audits, these controls have the highest failure rates.
            Pay special attention during your gap analysis:
        </p>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating critical"><i class="fas fa-times-circle"></i> Critical</span> A.5.7 - Threat
            Intelligence</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Organizations claim they "monitor threats" but lack structured processes.
            Reading security news isn't threat intelligence.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Documented threat intelligence sources and feeds</li>
            <li>Process for analyzing and actioning threat information</li>
            <li>Evidence of threat briefings to relevant stakeholders</li>
            <li>Integration with risk assessment and incident response</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="war-story-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> War Story: The "We Read The News" Defense</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                A financial services company confidently claimed A.5.7 compliance because their security team
                "follows industry news." The auditor asked for evidence of how a recent ransomware campaign
                affecting their sector was analyzed and actioned. Silence. The auditor found no documentation of
                threat sources, no analysis process, no evidence of sharing with IT teams. Result: Major
                non-conformity.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating critical"><i class="fas fa-times-circle"></i> Critical</span> A.6.3 - Security
            Awareness Training</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Annual checkbox training with no measurement of effectiveness. No
            role-based training. No evidence of behavior change.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Training program aligned to roles and risks</li>
            <li>Completion records with dates and attendee signatures</li>
            <li>Assessment/testing of knowledge retention</li>
            <li>Evidence of continuous reinforcement (phishing simulations, newsletters)</li>
            <li>Training updates when policies or threats change</li>
        </ul>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating high"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> High</span> A.8.9 -
            Configuration
            Management</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Organizations have configurations but no documented baselines. Drift from
            baseline isn't monitored. No approval process for changes.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Documented security baseline configurations for each technology</li>
            <li>Process to detect and remediate configuration drift</li>
            <li>Change management integration</li>
            <li>Regular configuration reviews (hardening assessments)</li>
        </ul>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating high"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> High</span> A.5.23 - Cloud
            Security</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Shadow IT, unclear responsibility models, treating cloud like
            on-premises.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Cloud service inventory and risk assessment</li>
            <li>Clear shared responsibility documentation per provider</li>
            <li>Cloud-specific security configurations and monitoring</li>
            <li>Exit strategy and data portability planning</li>
        </ul>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating high"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> High</span> A.8.16 - Monitoring
            Activities</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Logs exist but nobody reviews them. Alerts fire but nobody responds.
            No defined thresholds or escalation.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Defined monitoring requirements (what, where, how often)</li>
            <li>Alert thresholds and escalation procedures</li>
            <li>Evidence of log review (signed reviews, SIEM reports)</li>
            <li>Incident correlation and detection rules</li>
        </ul>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating medium"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Medium</span> A.8.28 -
            Secure
            Coding</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Developers say they follow secure coding, but no standards exist. No code
            review process. No security testing in CI/CD.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Documented secure coding standards (OWASP, SANS)</li>
            <li>Security code review process with records</li>
            <li>SAST/DAST integration in development pipeline</li>
            <li>Developer security training specific to languages used</li>
        </ul>

        <h3><span class="gap-rating medium"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Medium</span> A.5.22 -
            Supplier Monitoring</h3>
        <p>
            <strong>Why it fails:</strong> Initial assessment done, but no ongoing monitoring. No process for
            supplier changes or incidents.
        </p>
        <p><strong>What auditors look for:</strong></p>
        <ul>
            <li>Regular supplier security reviews (annual minimum)</li>
            <li>Monitoring of supplier security posture changes</li>
            <li>Notification requirements for supplier incidents</li>
            <li>Right to audit clauses exercised</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="scoring">6. Gap Scoring and Prioritization</h2>
        <p>
            Not all gaps are equal. Use a scoring matrix to prioritize remediation efforts:
        </p>

        <h3>Gap Severity Matrix</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Severity</th>
                    <th>Criteria</th>
                    <th>Remediation Priority</th>
                    <th>Timeline</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><span class="gap-rating critical"><i class="fas fa-times-circle"></i> Critical</span></td>
                    <td>Control not implemented; high risk exposure; will result in major NC</td>
                    <td>Immediate</td>
                    <td>0-30 days</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><span class="gap-rating high"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> High</span></td>
                    <td>Control partially implemented; significant gaps; likely minor NC</td>
                    <td>High</td>
                    <td>30-60 days</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><span class="gap-rating medium"><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Medium</span>
                    </td>
                    <td>Control mostly implemented; minor gaps; observation likely</td>
                    <td>Medium</td>
                    <td>60-90 days</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><span class="gap-rating low"><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Low</span></td>
                    <td>Control implemented; minor improvements possible; optimization</td>
                    <td>Low</td>
                    <td>90+ days</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Prioritization Formula</h3>
        <p>Calculate priority score for each gap:</p>
        <pre><code>Priority Score = (Risk Impact × Likelihood) + Audit Probability - Implementation Effort

Where:

  • Risk Impact: 1-5 (1=Low, 5=Critical)

  • Likelihood: 1-5 (1=Rare, 5=Almost Certain)

  • Audit Probability: How likely auditor will check (1-3)

  • Implementation Effort: Resource requirement (1-5, higher = harder)

          <p><strong>Example Calculation:</strong></p>
      <ul>
          <li>A.5.7 Threat Intelligence: (4 × 3) + 3 - 3 = 12 (High priority)</li>
          <li>A.8.28 Secure Coding: (3 × 2) + 2 - 4 = 4 (Medium priority)</li>
      </ul>

      <h2 id="remediation">7. Remediation Planning</h2>
      <p>
          Transform your gap findings into an actionable remediation plan:
      </p>

      <h3>Remediation Plan Template</h3>
      <table>
          <thead>
              <tr>
                  <th>Control</th>
                  <th>Gap Description</th>
                  <th>Action Required</th>
                  <th>Owner</th>
                  <th>Target Date</th>
                  <th>Status</th>
              </tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
              <tr>
                  <td>A.5.7</td>
                  <td>No formal threat intel process</td>
                  <td>Implement threat intel feeds, create analysis procedure</td>
                  <td>SOC Manager</td>
                  <td>Feb 28</td>
                  <td>In Progress</td>
              </tr>
              <tr>
                  <td>A.6.3</td>
                  <td>Training lacks role-based content</td>
                  <td>Develop role-specific training modules</td>
                  <td>HR/Security</td>
                  <td>Mar 15</td>
                  <td>Not Started</td>
              </tr>
              <tr>
                  <td>A.8.9</td>
                  <td>No baseline configurations documented</td>
                  <td>Create CIS-based baselines, implement drift detection</td>
                  <td>IT Ops</td>
                  <td>Apr 1</td>
                  <td>Planning</td>
              </tr>
          </tbody>
      </table>

      <h3>Quick Wins vs. Projects</h3>
      <p><strong>Quick Wins (1-2 weeks):</strong></p>
      <ul>
          <li>Documenting existing but undocumented processes</li>
          <li>Updating policies with missing sections</li>
          <li>Enabling existing but unused security features</li>
          <li>Creating missing forms and templates</li>
      </ul>
      <p><strong>Projects (1-3 months):</strong></p>
      <ul>
          <li>Implementing new technology controls (DLP, SIEM)</li>
          <li>Developing comprehensive training programs</li>
          <li>Establishing new processes (threat intelligence, secure development)</li>
          <li>Third-party risk management program build-out</li>
      </ul>

      <div class="success-box">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Best Practice: Evidence as You Go</strong>
          <p style="margin: 0;">
              As you remediate each gap, immediately collect and organize evidence. Don't wait until audit
              preparation. Create an evidence folder structure mirroring Annex A controls.
          </p>
      </div>

      <h2 id="war-stories">8. War Stories: Lessons from Real Assessments</h2>

      <div class="war-story-box">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> The Over-Confident CISO</strong>
          <p style="margin: 0.5rem 0;">
              A technology company's CISO was confident their existing SOC 2 controls would map directly to ISO
              27001. The gap analysis revealed 34 control gaps. SOC 2 covers security, but ISO 27001 includes
              physical security, HR processes, and supplier management that SOC 2 doesn't require. Lesson: Never
              assume framework equivalence without mapping.
          </p>
      </div>

      <div class="war-story-box">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> The Documentation Desert</strong>
          <p style="margin: 0.5rem 0;">
              A healthcare organization had excellent security practices but almost no documentation. Engineers
              knew what to do, but nothing was written down. The gap analysis found only 12 of 93 controls had
              adequate documentation. Six months of intensive documentation work followed. Lesson: Undocumented
              controls don't exist in an audit.
          </p>
      </div>

      <div class="war-story-box">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> The Shadow IT Surprise</strong>
          <p style="margin: 0.5rem 0;">
              During A.5.9 (asset inventory) assessment, the gap analysis team discovered 47 SaaS applications in
              use that IT knew nothing about. Marketing had procurement cards. Each unapproved app was a potential
              A.5.23 (cloud security) violation. The scope had to be expanded significantly. Lesson: Always do
              discovery before assuming you know your asset universe.
          </p>
      </div>

      <div class="war-story-box">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-skull-crossbones"></i> The Backup That Wasn't</strong>
          <p style="margin: 0.5rem 0;">
              For A.8.13 (backup), the IT team showed beautiful backup job success reports. The gap analyst asked
              for restore test evidence. Last restore test? 18 months ago. A test restore was performed during the
              assessment and failed. Backups had been completing but were corrupted. Lesson: Backup without tested
              restore is just storage.
          </p>
      </div>

      <h2 id="next-steps">10. Next Steps: From Gap to Certification</h2>
      <p>
          Your gap analysis is complete. Here's what comes next:
      </p>

      <h3>Immediate Actions (Week 1-2)</h3>
      <ol>
          <li>Present gap analysis findings to leadership</li>
          <li>Secure budget and resource commitment</li>
          <li>Assign control owners for each gap</li>
          <li>Prioritize quick wins for early momentum</li>
      </ol>

      <h3>Implementation Phase (Months 1-6)</h3>
      <ol>
          <li>Execute remediation plan in priority order</li>
          <li>Document everything as you implement</li>
          <li>Conduct mini internal audits to verify closure</li>
          <li>Update risk assessment with control improvements</li>
      </ol>

      <h3>Certification Preparation (Months 6-9)</h3>
      <ol>
          <li>Conduct full internal audit</li>
          <li>Management review meeting</li>
          <li>Address internal audit findings</li>
          <li>Select certification body and schedule audit</li>
      </ol>
